courses.title: Build and harden the identity foundation
courses.subtitle: AD DS, DNS, time, STIG hardening, PKI, DHCP & tiered administration
courses.description: Design the identity foundation with the government and vendor design references, then build it end to end: promote SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02, configure DNS and domain time, measure both controllers against the DISA STIG and harden them with Group Policy, build the two-tier PKI, stand up DHCP for VLAN 80 with secure DNS updates, and move administration onto tiered seats. Eight parts, each opening with its design decisions and closing with evidence for your portfolio.
outcomes: Design the forest, namespace, time hierarchy and PKI against government and vendor guidelines
Build and verify SBD-DC01, SBD-DC02, DNS and domain time
Measure against the DISA STIG and harden with Group Policy
Build the two-tier PKI, DHCP and tiered administration
courses.outcomeSummary: One forest on two healthy domain controllers, with DNS, domain time, a measured and hardened baseline, a two-tier PKI, DHCP and tiered administration, each designed against government and vendor guidelines and proven with evidence.

courses.title: Build the Linux repository on SBD-REPO01
courses.subtitle: Mirrored, signature-verified package snapshots for the Linux servers
courses.description: Build the one approved source of operating-system packages before any Linux server exists: verify the vendor's signing keys, build and harden SBD-REPO01 on VLAN 70 as a minimal web server, mirror and publish dated snapshots carried across the air gap and checked by hash and signature, write the client configuration every Linux server will use, and prove promotion, rollback and the first STIG baseline with the SCC for Linux set every Linux server is scanned with.
outcomes: Design the Linux package source: one Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family distribution, the repositories mirrored, verified upstream keys, and the register rows.
Build SBD-REPO01 as a hardened, minimal web server administered only from the Tier 1 seat.
Mirror, verify and publish dated snapshots, with promotion and rollback on record.
Hand later courses a tested client configuration that trusts only SBD-REPO01 and the verified keys.

stages.title: Design the repository and its trust
stages.detail: Before anything is mirrored, decide what SBD-REPO01 is for: the one approved source of operating-system packages for the domain-joined Linux servers, fed by dated snapshots whose upstream signing keys you verified first. Then place it on VLAN 70 and write its rows into the register.

stages.title: Build and harden SBD-REPO01
stages.detail: Build SBD-REPO01 as a minimal Linux server that does one job: answer package requests on TCP 80 and accept administration on SSH from one seat. Every other service, listener and account is left out.

stages.title: Mirror, verify, and publish a snapshot
stages.detail: The repository's content crosses the boundary like everything else: mirrored on the connected side, hashed, carried across, and checked twice on arrival, once against the hash manifest and once against the vendor's signatures. Only then is it published as a dated snapshot and entered in the catalog.

stages.title: Configure the Linux clients
stages.detail: Write the one client configuration every Linux server will use: a single source definition pointing at SBD-REPO01, the verified signing keys, and no other source. No consumer exists yet, so prove it on SBD-REPO01's own package manager and hand the files to courses 1.5 and 1.11.

stages.title: Keep it current and prove it
stages.detail: A repository is only as good as its last snapshot. Set the cadence that keeps it current, rehearse promoting a new snapshot and rolling back, stage SCC for Linux for every Linux server and take SBD-REPO01's first SCAP baseline with it, and close the course with a record an assessor can check.

courses.outcomeSummary: One verified source of Linux packages, ready before the first Linux server arrives.

courses.title: Collect the record on SBD-SYSLOG01
courses.subtitle: Design the logging pipeline and build its collector
courses.description: The first of three logging courses: design the whole collect → protect → analyze pipeline, then build its first stage — advanced audit policy on the DCs and admin hosts, source-initiated Windows Event Forwarding from every existing Windows system and a syslog intake on SBD-SYSLOG01, health checks with a named owner, and proof that real events arrive with the right names and times.
outcomes: Design all three logging stages: retention, readers, streams, and register rows.
Write the designed audit events on the DCs and admin hosts through GPO.
Forward every existing Windows system's events by source-initiated subscription and take syslog from the router and SBD-REPO01.
Keep the collector healthy and prove collection with events you cause.

stages.title: Design collect, protect, analyze
stages.detail: Three systems, three distinct jobs: SBD-SYSLOG01 gathers, SBD-AUDIT01 preserves, SBD-SPLUNK01 answers questions. This course builds the first; courses 1.4 and 1.5 build the other two — so decide now, for all three, what is collected, how long it lives, who may touch it, and where each stream is picked up.

stages.title: Turn on the right auditing
stages.detail: Forwarding garbage faster is not monitoring. Set the advanced audit policy so the events that tell the network's story — sign-ins, account changes, directory changes, policy changes — actually get written, at or above the STIG values course 1.1, part 4 measured.

stages.title: Build the collector
stages.detail: SBD-SYSLOG01 becomes the funnel: Windows Event Forwarding brings in the events of every Windows system that exists by source-initiated subscription, and a syslog receiver takes the core router's denies and, from lesson 5, the Linux servers over TLS — one host where the network's record first lands.

stages.title: Keep the collector trustworthy
stages.detail: A collector that silently stops is worse than none, because everyone assumes it works. Watch the subscription's runtime status, the sources that went quiet, the log's size and overwrite behavior, the disk, and the syslog intake — and decide who is told when collection fails.

stages.title: Prove collection and hand off
stages.detail: Prove the collector with events you cause on purpose: a failed sign-in, a denied probe, and a test message from SBD-REPO01, the first Linux source. Each must land with the right source name and time — then the cadence scans close the course.

courses.outcomeSummary: Every important event written, collected in one place, and proven to arrive with its true source and time.

courses.title: Protect the record on SBD-AUDIT01
courses.subtitle: Keep the audit record intact, even from its administrators
courses.description: The second of three logging courses: build SBD-AUDIT01 as the protected home for the collector's record — daily archives over encrypted SMB from a write-only managed account, SHA-256 hashes cataloged on arrival and verified every day, access auditing that leaves the box, retention that runs only as an approved and logged process, and proof that an administrator's delete is refused and a tampered copy is caught.
outcomes: Design and build the repository: retention, capacity, one write path, and the custodian's separate administration.
Archive the collector's streams daily over encrypted SMB from a write-only gMSA, with every archive hashed and cataloged.
Verify the catalog daily, audit access to the repository, and run retention as an approved, logged process.
Prove an administrator's delete is refused and logged, a tampered copy is caught, and an old archive can still be read.

stages.title: Design the repository and build SBD-AUDIT01
stages.detail: The repository has one job: keep the collector's record intact for its whole retention period, even from its own administrators. Size it, fix the one way in, name every identity and what it may do, and build SBD-AUDIT01 where the model puts it — before a single archive arrives.

stages.title: Archive, hash, and protect the record
stages.detail: The repository is where the record outlives mistakes and attackers alike: daily archives from the collector over an encrypted share, hashed before they leave and again on arrival, readable by few, and deletable by process only.

stages.title: Verify the catalog and watch the repository
stages.detail: A catalog nobody checks is a list of hopes. Re-hash every archive on a schedule, treat a mismatch as a finding, audit who reads or tries to change the repository, and keep the readers as few as the day they were approved.

stages.title: Run retention and prove retrieval
stages.detail: Retention cuts both ways: records must last the full period, and they must go when it ends — by a process with a log, never by a person's right-click. Run retention the way the design says, then prove the other half: an archive from the past can be found, verified, and read.

stages.title: Prove the record survives and hand off
stages.detail: Test the protection the way an attacker or a careless administrator would: try to delete an archive and tamper with a copy, and check that each attempt is refused or caught, and recorded. Then take SBD-AUDIT01's first baseline and hand the record to analysis.

courses.outcomeSummary: A record that arrives by one encrypted path, proves its own integrity every day, and outlives even its administrators.

courses.title: Analyze the record in SBD-SPLUNK01
courses.subtitle: Search a working copy, harden it, own the alerts, prove the chain
courses.description: The last of three logging courses: build SBD-SPLUNK01 as a single Splunk instance on domain-joined Linux patched only from SBD-REPO01, install Splunk Enterprise from hashed media, forward the collector's two streams over TLS, harden it to DISA's STIG, build the searches that answer this network's first questions, turn them and the pipeline's own failures into alerts someone owns, and trace one event from its source to the analyst's screen.
outcomes: Plan the single instance — indexes, retention, roles, console paths — and build SBD-SPLUNK01, patched only from SBD-REPO01.
Prepare the host, install Splunk, and forward the collector's streams over TLS, matching its counts and times.
Harden Splunk to DISA's STIG and record each item met another way.
Build working searches, and turn them and the pipeline's failures into tested alerts someone owns.
Trace one event from its source through the collector and the repository to the analyst's screen.

stages.title: Plan analysis and build SBD-SPLUNK01
stages.detail: Analysis works on a copy, not on the record: SBD-AUDIT01 keeps the evidence, and SBD-SPLUNK01 keeps a searchable working copy, for a period your environment sets, for the people who question them. Decide what the single instance holds, its indexes, retention, roles, and console paths first, then build the domain-joined Linux host that runs it — patched only from SBD-REPO01 and on domain time from its first boot.

stages.title: Prepare the host, install Splunk, and bring in the streams
stages.detail: Prepare SBD-SPLUNK01's hardened Linux for Splunk, then install Splunk Enterprise with the indexes, roles, and TLS receiving port lesson 1 designed, its indexes hashing every event from the first. Put a universal forwarder on SBD-SYSLOG01 that reads the collector's two streams and sends them over rule F10, and finish by proving the copy is faithful: Splunk's counts and times must match the collector's.

stages.title: Harden Splunk to the STIG
stages.detail: Splunk now holds the network's working copy, and DISA's Splunk Enterprise STIG says how it should behave. Before anyone else signs in, put the settings in place: the notice and session limits at the front door, sign-in with domain accounts over LDAPS, a free-space reserve the health report watches, and Splunk's audit trail under review. Then seal the install-time admin as the one local account, and record every STIG item this network meets another way.

stages.title: Build the working searches
stages.detail: Analysis earns its place with three working searches: failed privileged sign-ins, the boundary's denies, and the health of time — questions this network can already answer about itself. Build them as an analyst, prove each against an event you caused, and save them for the alerts in lesson 5.

stages.title: Own the alerts
stages.detail: An alert nobody owns is a log entry with extra steps. Turn the working searches and the pipeline's own failure conditions into scheduled alerts, each with a threshold set for your environment, a named responder, and a written first response; test each one by causing it, tune the noise, and set the review cadence AU-6 asks for.

stages.title: Prove the chain and hand off
stages.detail: One deliberate event, followed all the way: a failed privileged sign-in should appear on the source, the collector, the analyst's screen, and the repository's next-morning archive. That trace closes all three logging courses; SBD-SPLUNK01's first baseline and the handoff to the fleet close this one.

courses.outcomeSummary: A working copy that answers real questions, alerts someone owns, and one event traced through all three logging systems.

courses.title: Bring in the fleet
courses.subtitle: 50 Windows endpoints, managed from first boot
courses.description: Join the fifty-workstation fleet to a network that is ready for it: DHCP addressing, OU landing with STIG policy at first boot, Windows LAPS for every local administrator, certificate autoenrollment at scale, 802.1X port admission through NPS on SBD-DHCP01, and a sampled proof with the whole rollout observed by the logging pipeline.
outcomes: Roll fifty endpoints in waves that land hardened, addressed, and registered untouched.
Manage every local administrator with Windows LAPS under the tier model.
Admit only enrolled machines to VLAN 80 ports with 802.1X, proven in monitor mode before enforcement.
Prove the fleet with a defined sample, a failure rule, and pipeline-observed joins.

stages.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
stages.detail: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.

stages.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
stages.detail: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.

stages.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
stages.detail: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.

stages.title: Autoenroll the fleet's certificates
stages.detail: Course 1.1, part 6 proved autoenrollment on both domain controllers and its pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01; this lesson turns it loose. Widen the template permission to a fleet computer group, let the autoenrollment GPO already linked at the domain root do the enrolling, and verify a machine certificate chains and checks revocation across the boundary.

stages.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
stages.detail: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.

stages.title: Scale to fifty, enforce 802.1X, and prove by sample
stages.detail: Roll the remaining waves while the ports are still in monitor mode, confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates, then switch the ports to enforcement — and prove the fleet the only honest way at scale: a defined sample, the same checks as the pilot, and a written rule for what a sample failure means.

stages.title: Delta scan the fleet and hand off
stages.detail: The cadence meets its first population: the sampled endpoints get Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) baselines with the Windows client benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) copy, installed in course 1.1, part 8, the infrastructure this course changed is rescanned, and the fleet inventory is handed to course 1.8.

courses.outcomeSummary: Fifty endpoints that arrive hardened, certified, and watched from their very first sign-in.

courses.title: Deliver Windows updates from SBD-WSUS01
courses.subtitle: Air-gapped WSUS: offline import, four rings & Group Policy targeting
courses.description: Give every Windows system one road for updates: build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected WSUS server, feed it each month through the export and import path Microsoft describes for air-gapped networks, target four rings by Group Policy — pilot, workstations, member servers, then the domain controllers and the rest of Tier 0, installed by hand — and prove the cycle with WSUS reports, spot checks and a first STIG baseline.
outcomes: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected update server with TLS-protected metadata and tier-bound administration.
Carry each month's updates across the air gap by WSUS export and import, hashed on both sides.
Target four update rings with computer groups and Group Policy, with the domain controllers installed last and by hand.
Promote a monthly cycle ring by ring and prove it with compliance reports, spot checks and a first baseline.

stages.title: Design the rings and the Windows update rule
stages.detail: Decide how Windows updates reach the network before any arrive: one road through SBD-WSUS01, four rings that try every update on what the network can lose before what it can't, and a monthly crossing on the media procedure. Then confirm the register already carries the road.

stages.title: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected server
stages.detail: Build the server the network will take its updates from: a hardened member server on VLAN 20 that never synchronizes, serves metadata over TLS and signed files over HTTP, and is administered only from the two seats the tier model allows. Its scope is decided here, because what crosses each month is whatever that scope holds.

stages.title: Carry updates across the air gap
stages.detail: SBD-WSUS01 never talks to Microsoft. Each month a second WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the recorded scope and downloads its files; its metadata export and content folder cross on approved media, hashed on both sides, and SBD-WSUS01 imports them — the two-server path Microsoft describes for air-gapped networks.

stages.title: Target the rings with computer groups and Group Policy
stages.detail: Rings become mechanics: a computer group per ring on SBD-WSUS01, plus one for SBD-AUDIT01, client-side targeting so each computer files itself into its ring, and one Group Policy object per ring that names the server, the ring and its install behaviour. The domain controllers get a ring of their own: they download on their own but install only when Tier 0 starts it, and SBD-AUDIT01 waits for its audit custodian the same way.

stages.title: Run the first cycle and prove it
stages.detail: The design meets a real month: approve the imported updates for the pilot, promote them ring by ring on the written soak times, and install the domain controllers by hand. Then prove the result with WSUS's own reports, spot checks on the systems themselves, and the first SCAP baseline of SBD-WSUS01.

courses.outcomeSummary: One road for Windows updates: imported across the air gap, approved ring by ring, and proven.

courses.title: Keep the living inventory on SBD-MGMT01
courses.subtitle: Component inventory, discovery sources & monthly reconciliation
courses.description: Turn course 1.6's fleet snapshot into a living component inventory for the whole network: build SBD-MGMT01 on VLAN 70 as a keeper that reaches into nothing, record every component once with an accountable owner, check the record against what the directory, DHCP, WSUS and SBD-REPO01 already know, and reconcile it every month so drift becomes a finding.
outcomes: Define the inventory's boundary, columns and owners so every component is counted once and accountable.
Build SBD-MGMT01 as a hardened keeper administered only from the Tier 1 seat.
Gather discovery sources through existing administration paths and know what each one proves.
Reconcile recorded and discovered components every month, with a planted test proving detection works.

stages.title: Design the inventory and its keeper
stages.detail: Decide what the component inventory must hold before SBD-MGMT01 exists: every component inside the boundary counted once, and the columns that make each one accountable. Then name the records that can contradict it, and give it a keeper that holds the record without reaching into anything else.

stages.title: Build and harden SBD-MGMT01
stages.detail: Build the inventory's keeper as a small, quiet member server, joined into the Servers OU so the hardening, tier and update policies apply from its first boot. It answers only the Tier 1 seat, and the record sits on its own volume behind permissions that admit administrators alone.

stages.title: Build the living inventory
stages.detail: Course 1.6's fleet inventory was a snapshot of fifty PCs; SBD-MGMT01 makes the whole network's inventory a living record. Every component gets its place, ring, update source, baseline and owner, kept current by the procedures that change it.

stages.title: Feed it from what the network already knows
stages.detail: The inventory says what should exist; the network's own records say what does. Export the directory's computer objects, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions through the sessions administrators already use, and file them on SBD-MGMT01 with hashes, in one shape lesson 5 can compare.

stages.title: Reconcile the inventory and prove it
stages.detail: Compare the record with what the network reports, classify every difference, and prove the comparison catches drift before trusting a clean result. Then take SBD-MGMT01's first SCAP baseline and hand a reconciled inventory — and the monthly habit — to the courses that follow.

courses.outcomeSummary: One record of every component, checked every month against what the network itself reports.

courses.title: Endpoint protection on SBD-EPO01
courses.subtitle: Managed agents, protection policy & DLP from one console
courses.description: Managed endpoint protection and data-loss prevention for every Windows system, run from the single Trellix ePolicy Orchestrator server, SBD-EPO01.

courses.title: Credentialed scanning with SBD-NESSUS01
courses.subtitle: Scoped scan accounts, findings triage & the standing cadence
courses.description: Credentialed vulnerability scanning of the approved target list from the single Nessus server, SBD-NESSUS01, on domain-joined Linux.

courses.title: Stand up the business services
courses.subtitle: Files, database, licensing & web — by documented paths
courses.description: Give the users what the network exists for: SBD-FS01's role-based shares over verified SMB security, SBD-WEB01 serving internal HTTPS from a hardened, domain-joined Linux Apache, SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API, and SBD-SQL01 running as a managed identity behind exactly one caller — every hop a documented, proven register row.
outcomes: Serve files through role-group permissions with verified SMB signing and encryption.
Run the database as a managed identity, certificate-encrypted, with SBD-APPS01 as its only caller.
Prove the fleet → web → application → database chain with every hop registered and every shortcut denied.

stages.title: Design the service paths and identities
stages.detail: Four services, and before any of them exist: who talks to what over which port, which identity each service runs as, and which groups own access — the register and the directory answer all three before a role installs.

stages.title: Build SBD-FS01 with least-privilege shares
stages.detail: The file server is where access control meets daily life. Build the shares against the role groups, require SMB signing on the server instead of trusting client defaults, and make 'who can read this' a one-lookup question.

stages.title: Build SBD-SQL01 behind its applications
stages.detail: The database runs as a managed identity, encrypts its connections with a real certificate, and answers exactly one caller, SBD-APPS01 — the narrowest audience on the network, by design.

stages.title: Build SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01
stages.detail: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.

stages.title: Reconcile, scan, and hand off
stages.detail: The business services close the way every build course has: the register reconciled against live behavior, the new systems baselined, the inventory updated — and for the first time, the network is functionally complete.

courses.outcomeSummary: Files, licensing, and a three-tier web application, each reachable only by its documented path.

courses.title: Prove you can recover
courses.subtitle: Backups with custody, one rehearsed restore & the closing record
courses.description: Close the Build path by proving the network can come back: every backup in the network defined and scheduled in one place — the directory, the CA under ceremony-grade custody, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log archive, and the living records — in one hashed catalog, a timed restore rehearsal in isolation, and the recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence.
outcomes: Define and schedule every backup in the network — directory, CA, policy, DHCP, repository, analysis configuration, business services, logs, and records — in one verified catalog.
Rehearse a real system state restore in isolation, measured against written objectives.
File the tested-recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence for path 2.

stages.title: Decide what recovery must prove
stages.detail: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take, and the one schedule that says how each is backed up — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.

stages.title: Back up Tier 0: directory, CA, and policy
stages.detail: The Tier 0 rows of the schedule: system state from both controllers, the issuing CA under ceremony-grade protection, and the whole Group Policy estate with its links — plus the quiet feature that handles the most common 'disaster' of all: the Recycle Bin for deleted directory objects.

stages.title: Back up the member servers and records
stages.detail: The rest of the schedule: SBD-DHCP01 and the inventory, SBD-REPO01 and SBD-SPLUNK01, and the business services — SBD-FS01's shares with their permissions, SBD-SQL01's databases with the logins they depend on, SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates — then the log archive and the boundary's records, all in one hashed catalog.

stages.title: Carry the copies to the offline cabinet
stages.detail: A backup that sits on the server it protects fails with it. Move a copy of each backup to the offline cabinet by hand, under the same custody rules as any media crossing a boundary, and keep the custody record that proves it.

stages.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
stages.detail: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.

stages.title: File the recovery record and close the path
stages.detail: The Build path ends the way it worked: owners, schedules, and evidence. The recovery record joins the living documents, the closing SCAP results snapshot the finished network, and the Body of Evidence is ready for the authorization courses to assemble.

courses.outcomeSummary: Backups with custody, one real restore performed in isolation, and the evidence that you can come back.

courses.title: RMF to ATO
courses.subtitle: Every RMF step: the lessons, the workspace and the templates
courses.description: Take the network the Build the Network courses (1.1–1.12) create, the system shown in the System Hub, through all seven steps of the Risk Management Framework (RMF) to an Authorization to Operate, following NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 with the April 2016 Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) mapped in. Each step pairs its lessons with the same task in the ATO Package Builder and its templates from the ATO Template Library: prepare and categorize the system, select and implement its controls, build the Body of Evidence, assess it and plan the fixes in a POA&M, assemble the package for a decision, and keep the authorization current.
outcomes: Explain RMF roles and how NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 and the 2016 JSIG organize the seven steps and their outputs.
Prepare, categorize and select controls for the System Hub system, then implement them and prove each one with indexed evidence.
Assess the controls, plan every weakness in a POA&M, and take the package through review to an Authorizing Official's decision.
Keep the authorization current with change analysis, ongoing assessment and reporting, using official templates and practice samples at every step.

stages.title: RMF roles, steps, and editions
stages.detail: Explain who performs, assesses, and approves Risk Management Framework (RMF) work, and how NIST and the Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) organize its steps and outputs.
lessons: 01.3 NIST, the JSIG, and their editions

stages.title: Define and register the system
stages.detail: Establish what is being authorized and why: the mission, stakeholders, assets, boundary, information and its life cycle, early risks, and requirements. Then register the system.

stages.title: Describe and categorize the system
stages.detail: Describe the system, justify its confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts in the draft System Security Plan (SSP), and route the categorization for approval. Treat privacy applicability as an explicit decision.

stages.title: Select controls and plan monitoring
stages.detail: Turn the approved categorization into a selected, tailored, and allocated control set, with a draft Risk Assessment Report and a continuous monitoring strategy, ready for plan review and approval.

stages.title: Implement and document the controls
stages.detail: Implement the selected controls and record them as built in the System Security Plan (SSP) and Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM), in statements an assessor can test.

stages.title: Connect implementation to proof
stages.detail: Collect technical and operational evidence of the as-built system, index it, and correct the SSP and SCTM wherever the evidence and the plan disagree.
lessons: 06.3 The evidence index and the as-built plan

stages.title: Prepare the assessment
stages.detail: Select an independent assessor, hand over current evidence, and get a Security Assessment Plan approved before any testing starts.

stages.title: Perform and report the assessment
stages.detail: Assess the controls as planned, report supported findings in a Security Assessment Report (SAR), and remediate and reassess what can be fixed now.

stages.title: Build the plan of action and milestones
stages.detail: Turn the findings still open into a risk-ranked Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) with accountable owners, resources, dated milestones, and closure criteria.

stages.title: Assemble the authorization package
stages.detail: Assemble an authorization package whose plans, assessment results, and open risks agree, and submit it for the authorizing official’s decision.
lessons: 10.1 Package contents in the JSIG and NIST

stages.title: Support the authorization decision
stages.detail: Brief the risk the authorizing official must determine, propose a response to each significant risk, and record what an authorization decision contains.

stages.title: Monitor and maintain authorization
stages.detail: Keep the authorization true as the system changes: analyze each change, assess and report as the strategy requires, support ongoing authorization, and plan disposal.

relatedResources.title: Open the ATO Package Builder Hub
relatedResources.detail: Do each step on your Secure By Design enclave: register, categorize, implement, assess, authorize and monitor

relatedResources.title: Open the ATO Template Library
relatedResources.detail: Official sources and Secure By Design training samples for every step

relatedResources.title: Open the evidence workspace
relatedResources.detail: Fourteen practice artifacts, with blank starters in the workbook

courses.outcomeSummary: One system, taken from registration to a current Authorization to Operate: the lessons for each RMF step, the same work done in the ATO Package Builder, and the templates each step uses.

categories.title: Build the Network
categories.description: Build the complete air-gapped network, one system at a time: the domain controllers, DNS, domain time, STIG measurement and Group Policy hardening, the two-tier PKI, DHCP, tiered administration, the Linux repository, the logging pipeline (collector, protected archive, and analysis), the workstation fleet, Windows updates, the living inventory, business services, and proven recovery. Follow the courses in order, from 1.1 to 1.19.

categories.title: Network Authorization
categories.description: Take the network through all seven Risk Management Framework steps of NIST SP 800-37, with the JSIG mapped in, to an Authorization to Operate. One course: each step's lessons, the same task in the ATO Package Builder, and the templates it uses. Start after the network build.

categories.title: Templates & References
categories.description: Free, publicly released references to keep beside you while you build the Body of Evidence. Use them with any course, or on your own system.

categories.title: Government & Vendor Guidelines
categories.description: How to design each infrastructure service before you build it, from official vendor documentation and government and standards guidance: Microsoft, NIST, CISA, NSA, DISA, CIS, the IETF and ICANN. Each reference walks the design decisions, what each authority says, the trade-offs, and where the authorities agree, differ or conflict, with an annotated catalog of the sources behind it.

Each one is verified as publicly released by its publisher, and every link opens the publisher's own copy. Secure By Design training samples cover the documents that have no public version. references.title: Active Directory design
references.subtitle: Forest, domain, OU, trust, Group Policy and tiering design
references.description: Six design areas for the identity foundation: forest, domain, trusts, OU, Group Policy and administrative tiering. Microsoft supplies the structural logic; CISA/NSA, DISA and NIST supply the security overlay. Each area walks the decision at stake, the realistic options, what the government and vendor guidelines say, the trade-offs and the conflicts, with the annotated catalog of the Microsoft, NIST, CISA/NSA, DISA, CIS and IETF sources behind it.
references.outcomeSummary: The forest is the security boundary; design the forest, domain and OU structure for delegation and policy, then isolate the directory’s control plane as Tier 0.
outcomes: Decide how many forests and domains, and why the forest is the boundary
Design OUs for delegation and Group Policy, not replication
Keep Group Policy few and well-scoped, and deliver the baselines through it
Treat the directory’s control plane as Tier 0 with privileged access workstations

references.title: DNS design
references.subtitle: Namespace, zones, resolution, dynamic update, DNSSEC and logging design
references.description: Eight design areas for the name service Active Directory depends on: namespace, zones, resolution and forwarding, dynamic update, DNSSEC and integrity, availability and placement, hardening by design, and logging. Microsoft documents the Windows implementation; NIST SP 800-81r3, the DISA STIG, CISA and NSA set the security expectations, and the IETF and ICANN define the protocol. The annotated source catalog follows.
references.outcomeSummary: Name the forest under a domain you control, store zones in the directory with secure updates only, run two servers on different hosts, and decide DNSSEC, forwarding and logging by policy.
outcomes: Choose the namespace: a registered subdomain or ICANN’s reserved .internal, never .local
Store zones in the directory with secure dynamic updates only
Decide forwarding, root hints, protective DNS and encrypted DNS deliberately
Know where NIST, DISA and Microsoft disagree on dedicated servers, split DNS and DNSSEC

references.title: Time synchronization design
references.subtitle: The time hierarchy, upstream sources, Kerberos skew and virtualized controllers
references.description: Eight design areas for the service Kerberos, certificates and log correlation all depend on: the time hierarchy, upstream source selection, accuracy and performance, Kerberos skew, virtualized domain controllers, time authentication, Secure Time Seeding, and monitoring and leap seconds. Microsoft, NIST, NSA, CISA, DISA, CIS and the IETF are compared, with the annotated source catalog behind them.
references.outcomeSummary: Keep the domain time hierarchy: the forest-root PDC emulator is the reliable source, everything else follows the domain, virtual controllers never take time from the host, and Kerberos keeps its five-minute tolerance.
outcomes: Keep the default hierarchy with the PDC emulator as the one reliable source
Pick upstream sources by the authority you answer to: USNO or NIST, two to four of them
Hold the Kerberos skew at five minutes and plan accuracy around it
Stop virtualized controllers from taking time from their host

references.title: PKI design
references.subtitle: CA hierarchy, cryptography, validity, revocation, templates and CA protection
references.description: Ten design areas for the certificate services the lab builds in course 1.1, part 6: CA hierarchy, CA type and role, cryptography, validity and renewal, revocation and publication, certificate templates, enrollment, identity binding, CA protection and auditing, and logging. Microsoft, NIST, CISA/NSA and DISA are compared area by area, with the annotated source catalog behind them.
references.outcomeSummary: An offline standalone root with online enterprise issuing CAs, publication URLs fixed before the first certificate, renewal at half-life, and the whole PKI treated as Tier 0.
outcomes: Choose a two-tier hierarchy and add a policy tier only for a concrete need
Set key sizes, algorithms and validity periods from NIST SP 800-57
Fix CDP and AIA publication before the first certificate is issued
Design templates, enrollment and CA protection as Tier 0

references.title: DHCP design
references.subtitle: Placement, availability, scopes, options, DNS integration, hardening and logging
references.description: Eight design areas for the addressing service: server placement and authorization, high availability, scopes and the address plan, options, DNS dynamic-update integration, security and hardening, DHCPv6 and dual stack, and logging and the database. Microsoft documents the Windows service; NIST, DISA, CIS and the IETF set the security and protocol expectations. The annotated source catalog follows.
references.outcomeSummary: Run DHCP on dedicated, directory-authorized servers, plan scopes and failover, register names securely with one non-privileged credential, and leave spoofing protection to the switch and hypervisor.
outcomes: Place the service on dedicated domain members authorized in the directory
Design scopes, options and high availability for the address plan
Integrate with DNS through Name Protection and one dedicated credential
Protect against rogue servers at the switch and hypervisor, and keep the audit trail
